$comment: WHAT A PUBLISHED OPENAPI DOCUMENT MAY NEVER CARRY. One registry, two enforcers.
Read by ragcore/src/ragcore/api/openapi.py and by
dotnet/tests/Synthia.ContractTests/OpenApiEmissionTests.cs. Both stacks publish contracts, so
both apply the same list — two hand-maintained copies drift, and the drift is invisible until
the weaker of the two is the one that mattered.
IT LIVES IN A DATA FILE FOR A SECOND REASON. These terms are the shapes a credential takes, so
a list of them written as string literals in application source is indistinguishable, to a
secret scanner, from the credentials it is describing. tests/security/test_azure_identity.py
found exactly that and was right to: a policy list and a leaked key look the same from the
outside. Keeping the vocabulary as data rather than as code resolves it without weakening
either guard.
MATCHED AGAINST NAMES, NEVER DESCRIPTIONS. A document explaining that an operation carries no
credential is correct documentation; a field called apiKey is a defect whatever it holds today.
A scanner that flagged the prose would get the prose deleted, and then nobody remembers why.

secretTerms.$comment: Substring match against a normalised name. 'api_key', 'apiKey' and 'api-key' all reduce to 'apikey'.

$comment: Exact match against a normalised name, not substring: 'roles' must not be a parameter, but a
schema called 'AcceptedRolesSummary' is a legitimate read model and a substring rule would
reject it.
Two different things are in this list, and they are enforced differently. implementationDetail
is forbidden ANYWHERE in a document — a client that can see it starts depending on it, and then
the detail is a contract nobody agreed to. derivedAuthority is forbidden only where a CLIENT
CAN SUPPLY IT; see below.
WHERE derivedAuthority NAMES ARE FORBIDDEN, AND WHY IT IS A POSITION RULE RATHER THAN A NAME
RULE. The platform derives tenant, roles and audience and never accepts them (constitution P-I,
contracts §README rule 1). What must not exist is a way for a client to ASSERT one — a request
parameter or a request-body field. Publishing one advertises exactly what the platform refuses,
and a client that sent it would get a silent no-op rather than an error, which is the worst of
both.
A RESPONSE IS THE OPPOSITE CASE. 'vw_session_summary_v1' carries tenant_id and the read model
that maps it carries tenantId; that is the organisation a row BELONGS to, reported back to a
caller already entitled to the row. Forbidding the name there would force a read model to hide
which organisation an audit record concerns, which is the field a staff reviewer is reading it
for. The earlier flat name rule did exactly that, and would have been satisfied by renaming the
field rather than by removing an authority channel — the shape of a rule that looks enforced
and is not.
SO: forbidden in a parameter or a request body, permitted in a response.
THE ONE EXCEPTION IS NAMED, SCOPED AND JUSTIFIED. contracts §README declares tenantId a
staff-only NARROWING: it selects within the set the caller may already see, reaching the query
as one more WHERE clause underneath the global scope filter, so a caller naming an organisation
outside their scope receives no rows rather than that organisation's rows. It narrows; it
cannot widen. It is permitted as a QUERY parameter on the STAFF documents and nowhere else —
not on customer, not on workload, and never in a body, a header or a path.

exceptions.name: tenantId
exceptions.reason: Staff-only narrowing within the caller's existing scope; contracts/README.md.

structuralKeys.$comment: Keys of the OpenAPI format itself, skipped. 'security' and 'securitySchemes' describe HOW to authenticate and never with what.
